Macedonia
mass-uh-DOH-nee-uh
noun (place)
Greek Makedonia, the kingdom of Philip and Alexander; later the Roman province north of Achaia in the Balkan peninsula.

📖 Biblical Definition

Macedonia is the Roman province lying north of Achaia in the Greek peninsula, the first soil of Europe to receive the gospel. It was to Macedonia that Paul was summoned by the night vision, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us" (Acts 16:9), and in obedience he crossed from Troas to plant churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea. There Lydia's heart was opened, the Philippian jailor cried, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?", and the noble Bereans "searched the scriptures daily." The Macedonian churches, though tried by deep affliction, became a wonder of liberality, for Paul testifies, "how that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality" (2 Cor 8:2). They gave "beyond their power" and first "gave their own selves to the Lord" (2 Cor 8:5). Thus Macedonia stands in Scripture both as the gateway of the gospel into Europe and as a pattern of grace-wrought generosity. This dictionary confesses that the same sovereign Lord who directed Paul's steps to Macedonia wrought in her poor saints a liberality that shames the rich.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Roman province north of Achaia in the Greek peninsula; the first region of Europe evangelized by Paul, home to the churches of Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, renowned for their grace-wrought liberality.

expand to see more

MACEDONIA, noun. A Roman province in the north of the Greek peninsula, above Achaia.

The first part of Europe to hear the gospel, entered by Paul after the vision, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us."

Its chief gospel cities were Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea.

Its churches, in deep poverty, abounded in liberality: "to their power, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves."

A standing example of giving that flows first from giving one's own self to the Lord.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 16:9 — "And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us."

2 Cor 8:1 — "Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia."

2 Cor 8:2 — "How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality."

2 Cor 8:5 — "And this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the lesson to recover is that true Christian liberality springs from grace, not surplus.

expand to see more

Macedonia is a place-name with no modern ideological redefinition, yet the modern church often inverts its lesson. The prevailing assumption is that giving follows prosperity—that men give when they have plenty. The Macedonians give the lie to this: in "deep poverty" and "great trial of affliction" their joy overflowed in liberality "beyond their power." Generosity is fruit of grace, not of abundance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order Paul names: they "first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God." Christian liberality is not a fundraising technique but the overflow of hearts already surrendered to Christ. Where the self is given, the purse follows; where it is withheld, no campaign can manufacture the grace. Macedonia summons the affluent church to repentance and to the joy of giving that springs from grace.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Greek Makedonia, the ancient kingdom and later Roman province north of Achaia.

expand to see more

Greek Makedonia named the kingdom of Philip II and Alexander the Great.

Under Rome it became a senatorial province with capital at Thessalonica.

The man of the vision is called aner Makedon, a Macedonian, in Acts 16:9.

Paul's letters to Philippi and Thessalonica address Macedonian churches directly.

The province roots the European church's beginnings in apostolic, Spirit-led missions.

Usage

"Paul preached in Macedonia before passing southward into Achaia and the city of Corinth."

"The churches of Macedonia, though poor, gave so liberally that Paul held them up as an example to Corinth."

"Lydia of Thyatira was the first convert in Macedonia, her heart opened by the Lord at Philippi."
